Treasury Financing Operations
December Certificate and Bond
Naturities

On November 19, 1947, the Secretary of the Treasury announced the plans to refund the $3,982 million of securities maturing in December. The maturing securities consisted of a one-year 7/8 percent certificate of indebtedness maturing December 1 in the amount of $3,281 million and the 2 percent bonds of 1947 maturing December 15, 1947, in the amount of $701 million.

In exchange for the two maturing issues, there was offered an issue of 13-month Treasury notes, dated December 1, 1947, and bearing interest from that date at the rate of 1-1/8 percent per annum, payable with the principal at maturity on January 1, 1949. In the case of the maturing certificates, exchanges were made par for par, and in the case of the maturing bonds, exchanges were made at par with an adjustment of interest as of December 15, 1947. The notes were issued in bearer form only, in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $10,000, $100,000, and $1,000,000.

Reports to the Treasury on the ownership of Government securities indicate that on October 31, 1947, about 29 percent of the $3,281 million of certificates maturing December 1, and about 74 percent of the $701 million of 2 percent bonds maturing December 15 were owned by reporting commercial banks and Federal Reserve Banks. The ownership figures for October 31 are the latest which are available for holdings of both commercial banks and Federal Reserve Banks.

Subscription books were opened on November 19 and closed at the close of business November 28. Holdings of the certificates of indebtedness by the Federal Reserve Banks, which amounted to $139 million, were redeemed in full for cash. Certificates of indebtedness subscribed in exchange for the new notes amounted to $2,908 million, leaving

$234 million to be paid in cash to holders other than Federal Reserve Banks. Bonds subscribed in exchange for the new notes amounted to $627 million, leaving $74 million to be paid in cash.
Treasury Bill Retirement in November

A further redemption in outstanding Treasury bills was made by the Treasury Department in November. The four issues maturing during the month totaled $4.8 billion and the total refunded was $4.4 billion. Each weekly maturing issue was reduced by $100 million. The first maturity was for $1.1 billion, the second and third for $1.2 billion each, and the fourth for $1.3 billion. Bill retirements from April 17, when the first bill reduction took place, through November 28, 1947, have totaled $1.7 billion. The average rates of discount for the four offerings, beginning with that dated November 6, were 0.895 percent, 0.912 percent, 0.931 percent, and 0.940 percent, respectively.
Call of Two Issues of Treasury Bonds

On November 14, 1947, the Secretary of the Treasury announced that two issues of Treasury bonds were called for redemption on March 15, 1948. These issues are the 2 percent Treasury bonds of 1948-50, dated March 15, 1941, and the 2-3/4 percent Treasury bonds of 1948-51, dated March 16, 1936. There are outstanding $1,115 million of the 2 percent bonds and $1,223 million of the 2-3/4 percent bonds. The interest on the 2 percent issue is taxable and on the 2-3/4 percent issue is partially tax exempt. The announcement stated that the holders of the bond issues may, in advance of the redemption date, be offered the privilege of exchanging all or any part of the called bonds for other interest-bearing obligations of the United States, in which event public notice would be given and an official circular governing the exchange offering would be issued.

Treasury Bulletin
Capital Movements Between the United States and Foreign Countries,
and Net Position in Foreign Currencies

This chapter on Capital Movements between the United States and Foreign Countries and Position in Foreign Currencies is divided into four main groups. Section I of Capital Movements, the Historical Summary, contains data regarding capital movements by the principal types of data, and by years from 1935, and currently by months. Each type of data is then broken down into its chief components in the same chronological detail.

Section II supplies a geographic breakdown by principal countries on a monthly basis. The total capital movements are given first and then the principal categories are shown separately. In addition, at this point, the total outstanding claims on and liabilities to foreign countries are each presented.
Details with respect to capital movements and short-term claims and liabilities are presented in Section III as of the latest month for which the data are available.
The last group contains monthly data regarding the
net position in foreign currencies of United States banks and brokers, their outstanding foreign exchange contracts, and purchases and sales of foreign exchange, both spot and forward.

These data are based on reports filed each month by banks, bankers, and brokers throughout the United States. The reports are collected, checked, and tabulated by the twelve Federal Reserve Banks. The totals are then forwarded to the Treasury Department for consolidation and publication.
Figures for previous periods may be obtained from the following sources:
Supplement to the 'Treasury Bulletin' on 'Capital Movements between the United States and Foreign Countries, January 1942 through April 1945', for details during that period.
"Treasury Bulletin", November 1945, for capital movements, and position in foreign currencies by months, 1942-1945.
Treasury Bulletins, March 1942 and earlier, for details covering years back to January 2, 1935.
